content: Idiopathic hypersomnia is a condition characterized by excessive sleepiness without an identifiable cause. Unlike narcolepsy, idiopathic hypersomnia does not involve sudden episodes of falling asleep or the loss of muscle control triggered by strong emotions, known as cataplexy. The symptoms of idiopathic hypersomnia often develop gradually during adolescence or early adulthood. These symptoms include daytime naps that fail to alleviate drowsiness, difficulty waking up from prolonged sleep (often accompanied by confusion or disorientation), and an increased need for sleep during the day, even during activities such as work, meals, or conversations. Individuals with this condition may sleep for extended periods, sometimes up to 14 to 18 hours per day. Additional symptoms may include anxiety, irritability, low energy levels, restlessness, slowed thinking or speech, reduced appetite, and memory difficulties. It is important to note that cataplexy, a hallmark symptom of narcolepsy, is not present in idiopathic hypersomnia. The causes of idiopathic hypersomnia are not well understood, and the diagnostic process typically involves ruling out other potential causes of excessive daytime sleepiness. Other sleep disorders that may lead to similar symptoms include isolated sleep paralysis, narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea, and restless leg syndrome. Non-sleep-related causes of excessive sleepiness may include atypical depression, certain medications, substance use (including drugs and alcohol), hypothyroidism (low thyroid function), and a history of head injury. To diagnose idiopathic hypersomnia, healthcare providers will take a detailed sleep history and may perform specific tests. These tests can include a multiple sleep latency test and a sleep study (polysomnography) to rule out other sleep disorders. A psychiatric evaluation may also be conducted to assess for atypical depression. Treatment for idiopathic hypersomnia often involves the use of stimulant medications such as amphetamine, methylphenidate, or modafinil. However, these medications may not be as effective for idiopathic hypersomnia as they are for narcolepsy. In addition to pharmacological treatment, certain lifestyle modifications can help manage symptoms and reduce the risk of injury. These include avoiding alcohol, refraining from operating motor vehicles or using dangerous machinery, and avoiding night shifts or social activities that delay bedtime.
